title: The straddle measures something else
lede: Page 08 established the identity in one line: a straddle costs about 0.7979·S·σ√T , so the implied move it quotes is about 80% of a one-sigma move. This page is about why that number is 0.7979, what happens when it is not, and what the difference does to a position.

chapters.title: Two rulers, one distribution
chapters.dek: Squaring the deviations before averaging them is a choice, and it produces a different number from not squaring them.

figures.title: The same distribution, measured twice
figures.caption: The green line sits inside the red one, always, and by a fixed 20% for a normal. Everything on this page is a consequence of that gap.

checks.q: Why is the standard deviation always at least as large as the mean absolute deviation?
checks.right: Because squaring before averaging weights large deviations more heavily, and the root does not undo that reweighting
checks.why: The squaring reweights before the averaging. This is Jensen's inequality doing the work — the root of a mean of squares is never below the mean of the absolute values, with equality only when every deviation is identical. It is also why the standard deviation is the more fragile of the two under fat tails, which is chapter 05.

terms.Mean absolute deviation: The average of the absolute distances from the mean, with no squaring. A measure of spread in its own right, not an approximation to the standard deviation — and the one an option payoff actually references.

chapters.text: Ask how spread out a distribution is and there are two honest answers. Average the absolute deviations, or average the squared deviations and take the root. Both are legitimate; neither is an approximation to the other. The second is the standard deviation , and it dominates finance for reasons that are mostly about convenience: variances add, so a two-day variance is twice a one-day variance and the √T scaling of page 01 follows immediately. Absolute deviations do not add like that, which is why nobody builds a model on them. The first is the mean absolute deviation . It has no such algebra, but it has something else: it is what an option pays. A straddle held to expiry pays |S_T − K| , an absolute value with no square in sight. Because squaring weights the far observations more heavily, the standard deviation always comes out the larger of the two. For a normal distribution the ratio is √(2/π) = 0.797885 , and it is worth seeing where that comes from — it is the average of |z| under a standard normal, which is a one-line integral rather than a fitted constant. The same distribution, measured twice Controls The green line sits inside the red one, always, and by a fixed 20% for a normal. Everything on this page is a consequence of that gap. [equation: MAD = E|X − μ| σ = √( E[(X − μ)²] ) for a normal, MAD = √(2/π)·σ ≈ 0.7979·σ] Reads as: average the distances, or average the squared distances and take the root. The squaring is what makes the second larger, because it pays disproportionate attention to the observations far from the middle. chapters.title: What a straddle actually buys
chapters.dek: The payoff is an absolute value, so the price is an expected absolute move. The screen then quotes it next to a volatility, which is a standard deviation.

figures.title: The exact straddle, the approximation, and the sigma behind them
figures.caption: The blue and red lines are indistinguishable at any realistic vol-time — the approximation is high by 0.03% at 30 vol and 30 days. The gold line is 25% above both, and is what people mean when they say sigma.

checks.q: A screen shows an implied move of 5%. What is the one-standard-deviation move?
checks.right: 6.27%, being 5% ÷ 0.7979. The implied move is the expected absolute move, which is about 80% of a sigma
checks.why: 6.27%. And the difference matters for more than pedantry: at 5% you expect a breach 31.7% of the time and get 42.5%. Any comparison between a straddle-implied move and a historical standard deviation has to convert one to the other first, or it is off by a quarter before it starts.

chapters.text: A straddle struck at the forward pays |S_T − K| . Its price is therefore the expected absolute move, discounted — and under Black–Scholes that expectation has a closed form which, for realistic vol-times, is almost exactly 0.7979·S·σ√T . Take a concrete one. A 30-day straddle on a $100 stock at 30 vol costs $6.860 . Quoted as an implied move that is 6.86% of spot. The one-standard-deviation move over the same period is 0.30 × √(30/365) = 8.60% . The ratio of the two is 0.7976 , which is the theoretical 0.797885 to three decimals. So the conversions, both worth having automatic: Going from a quoted implied move to a volatility, divide by 0.7979 or multiply by 1.2533 . Going the other way, multiply by 0.7979. And treating the implied move as though it were one sigma understates the volatility by 20.2% of itself — or, from the other end, the true sigma is 25.3% larger than the number being quoted. The practical consequence is about frequency. If you think the implied move is one sigma you expect the stock to breach it 31.7% of the time. It actually breaches it 42.5% of the time, because the breakeven sits at 0.80 sigma rather than 1.00. That is a gap of nearly eleven percentage points in how often a straddle you bought finishes in the money, and it is the single most common miscalibration in reading an implied move. The exact straddle, the approximation, and the sigma behind them Controls The blue and red lines are indistinguishable at any realistic vol-time — the approximation is high by 0.03% at 30 vol and 30 days. The gold line is 25% above both, and is what people mean when they say sigma. [equation: σ = implied move ÷ 0.7979 = implied move × 1.2533 implied move = 0.7979 × σ] Reads as: the quoted move and the standard deviation differ by a fixed factor of about a quarter. Which one a sentence means is almost never stated, and the two get compared to each other constantly. Try this Push the volatility up and watch the approximation drift above the exact price. Find the vol where the error first exceeds a tenth of a percent.

chapters.title: 0.7979 is the normal's number, and nothing else's
chapters.dek: Change the shape of the tails and the ratio moves. For a t with six degrees of freedom it is exactly three quarters.

figures.title: The ratio, against how fat the tails are
figures.caption: The curve approaches 0.7979 from below as the degrees of freedom rise. Everything to the left of the gold line is a distribution for which the standard conversion understates the volatility.

checks.q: Two markets quote the same 5% implied move, but one has visibly fatter tails. Which has the higher standard deviation?
checks.right: The fat-tailed one. Its MAD-to-sigma ratio is lower, so the same expected absolute move implies a larger sigma — 7.07% against 6.27% at four degrees of freedom
checks.why: The fat-tailed one, by 12.8%. The straddle price pins the expected absolute move, and that is all it pins. Converting it to a standard deviation requires a distributional assumption, and the standard one — normality — is the assumption that produces the smallest answer of any realistic candidate.

chapters.text: Everything in chapter 02 assumed a normal distribution. The straddle price is an expectation of an absolute value and does not care what shape produced it — but the conversion to a standard deviation does, entirely. Under fatter tails the standard deviation is inflated by the extremes far more than the mean absolute deviation is, so the ratio between them falls . The exact values are unusually clean: A uniform distribution, with no tails at all, gives √3/2 = 0.8660 . The normal gives 0.7979 . A Student t with 6 degrees of freedom gives exactly 3/4 . A t with 4 gives exactly 1/√2 = 0.7071 , which is also the Laplace value. A t with 3 gives exactly 2/π = 0.6366 . Now put that to work. A straddle quotes a 5% expected absolute move. Under a normal that implies a volatility of 6.27% . If the true distribution is a t with 4 degrees of freedom — fat, but not absurd for a single name over a month — the same straddle implies 7.07% , which is 12.8% higher . The option price did not change. The number you wrote down next to it did. This is a real and underappreciated wedge. Every implied volatility on a screen was produced by inverting a model that assumes a normal distribution of log returns. To the extent the truth has fatter tails, the ATM implied vol is a statement about the expected absolute move dressed up as a statement about a standard deviation — and the two drift apart in exactly the situations, like a single name into a binary event, where you care most. The ratio, against how fat the tails are Controls The curve approaches 0.7979 from below as the degrees of freedom rise. Everything to the left of the gold line is a distribution for which the standard conversion understates the volatility. Where this comes from For a standardized Student t with ν degrees of freedom, the mean absolute deviation and the standard deviation both have closed forms: E|T| = 2√ν · Γ((ν+1)/2) ÷ ( √π · (ν−1) · Γ(ν/2) ) and σ = √( ν/(ν−2) ) , so the ratio is the first divided by the second. The gamma functions collapse at small integer ν, which is why the values come out as recognizable constants — 2/π at ν = 3, 1/√2 at ν = 4, exactly 3/4 at ν = 6 — and why the limit as ν grows is √(2/π), the normal's value, approached from below. Where it breaks: the standard deviation only exists for ν > 2, and the ratio is undefined below that — for a t with 2 degrees of freedom the variance is infinite while the mean absolute deviation is perfectly finite, so the straddle has a price and the volatility does not exist. That is not a pathology invented for a textbook; it is the formal version of the complaint that a single implied volatility cannot describe a distribution whose second moment is dominated by events that have not happened yet, which page 20 takes up directly. The Student t is also only a stand-in — real return distributions are skewed, and skew breaks the symmetry every formula here assumes.

chapters.title: Fat tails mean fewer wins, not more
chapters.dek: The straddle buyer's hit rate falls as the tails fatten. The payouts, when they come, get larger.

figures.title: How often the move is breached, against how fat the tails are
figures.caption: Two horizontal lines and a curve that sits between them. The distance from the grey line to the gold one is the error from confusing the two rulers; the slope of the red curve is the effect of the tails on top of it.

figures.title: Trade it on fat tails
figures.caption: With tails close to normal the buyer wins 41.9% of trades; at four degrees of freedom, 37.4%; at three, 35.1%. Every price is fair, so the averages stay at zero. What fat tails change is how the zero is made: the buyer loses more often and wins bigger, and the seller's worst trade in four thousand grows from $3,017 near the normal to $15,270 at four degrees of freedom, on a $1,000-per-sigma position.

checks.q: You buy a straddle in a market with fat tails. Compared to a normal market at the same price, what changes?
checks.right: You win less often — 37.4% against 42.5% at four degrees of freedom — and by more when you do
checks.why: Less often, and larger. Fat tails put more mass near zero as well as far out, and the near-zero mass is what determines the hit rate. This is also why a seller's high hit rate is not evidence of an edge — in the fattest-tailed markets it is a mechanical consequence of the shape, and the losses are waiting in the part of the distribution the hit rate does not describe.

chapters.text: Here is a result that runs against most people's instinct. If the distribution has fatter tails, does the stock exceed the straddle-implied move more often or less often? Less often. Under a normal, the breach rate is 42.49% . Under a t with 30 degrees of freedom it is 41.9% ; with 10, 40.7% ; with 6, 39.4% ; with 4, 37.4% . Under a Laplace distribution the answer is exactly e⁻¹ = 36.79% . The reason is that a fat-tailed distribution is not simply "more spread out." It is more concentrated in the middle and more spread in the extremes — that is what excess kurtosis means. The straddle prices the average absolute move, and the average is pulled upward by the rare large outcomes. So the breakeven sits further out relative to the bulk of the distribution, and the many quiet days fall short of it. For a straddle buyer this is the whole character of the trade in one number. Fatter tails do not make the position win more often; they make it lose small more often and win big less often . The expected value can be identical while the path is completely different, which is page 25 's distinction between an edge and a distribution of outcomes arriving in the most concrete possible form. And it explains something that otherwise looks like a puzzle: sellers of options report high hit rates in exactly the markets where their tail risk is worst. The hit rate is high because the tail is fat. Those are the same fact. How often the move is breached, against how fat the tails are Controls Two horizontal lines and a curve that sits between them. The distance from the grey line to the gold one is the error from confusing the two rulers; the slope of the red curve is the effect of the tails on top of it. Feel it from the trading side. Every straddle below is priced exactly at the expected absolute move of the distribution you choose, so on average neither side makes anything. Pick a side, set how fat the tails are, and trade. Watch how often you win, and what the worst trade looks like. Trade it on fat tails Your side With tails close to normal the buyer wins 41.9% of trades; at four degrees of freedom, 37.4%; at three, 35.1%. Every price is fair, so the averages stay at zero. What fat tails change is how the zero is made: the buyer loses more often and wins bigger, and the seller's worst trade in four thousand grows from $3,017 near the normal to $15,270 at four degrees of freedom, on a $1,000-per-sigma position. Trader's lens A trader who sells straddles and wins two times in three is not proving an edge; on fat tails that is what a fair price looks like. The edge, if there is one, is in the average after the big losses, so a seller is judged on the worst trade and a buyer on whether they can afford the long run of small losses before it. Win rate tells you the shape of a strategy, not its value. Fatter tails make selling look better month to month and worse in the year that matters. Price straddles from the distribution you believe, not from the normal's 0.7979. Rule of thumb: on a fairly priced straddle, the buyer should expect to lose more often than they win. chapters.title: Measuring volatility with absolute values
chapters.dek: The same choice, made on realized data rather than implied. One estimator is steadier and one is honest, and they are not the same one.

figures.title: Two estimators over many samples, clean and contaminated
figures.caption: Drag the contamination up from zero. The blue histogram widens and stays centered; the green one holds its width and walks to the left. Stability and honesty are trading against each other.

checks.q: A desk switches from squared returns to absolute returns for its realized-vol number and finds it reads consistently low. Is the new estimator broken?
checks.right: No. It is unbiased for the mean absolute deviation, and the 1.2533 conversion to sigma only holds for a normal. Fat tails make it read low by construction
checks.why: It is measuring the right thing and converting with the wrong constant. Exactly chapter 03's problem on realized data instead of implied. The estimator is faithful; the 1.2533 that turns it into a volatility assumes a shape the data does not have, and the shortfall is a rough measure of how far from normal the returns are.

chapters.text: The distinction is not only about pricing. Estimating realized volatility offers the identical choice: average the squared returns and take a root, or average the absolute returns and scale by √(π/2) = 1.2533 . Under a genuinely normal distribution the squared-return estimator wins, though not by much. Its sampling variance is σ²/2n against the absolute estimator's σ²(π/2 − 1)/n = 0.5708σ²/n , a relative efficiency of 87.6% — the absolute version needs 14.2% more data for the same precision. Its spread of estimates is wider by √((π/2 − 1) ÷ ½) = 1.068 , and the figure below resamples enough times to land there. Now contaminate it. Let 6% of days come from a distribution with four times the volatility — a mild version of what a real return series looks like. The true sigma is 1.3784 . The squared estimator still converges to it. The absolute estimator converges to 1.1800 — which is √(π/2) times the mixture's own expected absolute value, and works out to 85.6% of the truth. Meanwhile the spreads swap places: the squared estimator's roughly triples while the absolute one's barely moves, leaving it about half as wide. That is the trade, and it is not a free lunch in either direction. The absolute estimator is roughly twice as stable under contamination and biased low for the standard deviation, because it is faithfully measuring a different quantity — the mean absolute deviation — whose relationship to sigma just moved. The squared estimator remains unbiased and becomes wildly noisy. Neither is wrong. The question is which quantity you actually need. If you are sizing against a tail, you want the noisy unbiased one and you should expect it to jump around. If you are tracking whether today is busier than last week, the stable one is telling you what you asked, and its bias is a constant you can ignore. chapters.title: Drill it
chapters.dek: Converting between the two rulers, in both directions, until it is automatic.

figures.caption: Two constants carry this entire page: 0.7979 one way and 1.2533 the other. The third worth memorizing is 42.5%.

checks.q: What does a straddle held to expiry actually pay?
checks.right: The absolute value of the move, |S_T − K| — so its price is an expected absolute deviation, with no squaring anywhere in it
checks.why: An absolute value. Which is why the price references the mean absolute deviation rather than the standard deviation, and why a constant appears the moment you try to quote it as a volatility.

checks.q: A screen shows a 4% implied move. What is the one-sigma move?
checks.why: 5.01%. The third option applies the conversion backwards, which is the error to watch for — 0.7979 takes you from sigma to the implied move, and 1.2533 takes you back.

checks.q: How often does the stock breach the straddle-implied move, under a normal distribution?
checks.right: 42.5%, because the breakeven sits at 0.80 sigma rather than 1.00
checks.why: 42.5%. The first option is the answer to a different question — how often a genuine one-sigma move is breached — and the eleven-point gap between them is the practical cost of confusing the two rulers.

checks.q: For a Student t with six degrees of freedom, what is the ratio of MAD to sigma?
checks.right: Exactly 3/4 — lower than the normal, because fatter tails inflate sigma more than they inflate the MAD
checks.why: Exactly three quarters. The ratio is a property of the distribution's shape, not a universal constant: 0.8660 for a uniform, 0.7979 for a normal, 3/4 at six degrees of freedom, 1/√2 at four and 2/π at three.

checks.q: Fatter tails, same straddle price. Does the stock breach the implied move more or less often?
checks.right: Less often. 37.4% at four degrees of freedom against 42.5% for a normal, because the extra mass sits near zero as well as far out
checks.why: Less often, and bigger when it does. This is why a high hit rate on short options is not evidence of an edge — in the fattest markets it is a mechanical property of the shape, and the losses live in the part of the distribution a hit rate does not describe.

checks.right: It depends what you need. RMS is unbiased for sigma and noisy under contamination; 1.2533×mean|r| is about twice as stable and reads 85.6% of the truth once tails appear
checks.why: Neither dominates. Under a clean normal the absolute estimator is 87.6% as efficient as RMS — worse, but only just. Under contamination the absolute estimator is far steadier and biased low, because it is faithfully measuring a mean absolute deviation whose conversion to sigma has changed underneath it.
